soil-bio-001.title: The crowded underworld that keeps soil alive
soil-bio-001.text: Soil is home to circa 59% of the world's biodiversity. Soil biology is the study of the activity and ecology of the microbes and animals that live there. Its subject is soil life, also called soil biota or edaphon. That covers every organism that spends a significant part of its life cycle in the soil profile or at the soil-litter interface. The cast runs from bacteria, fungi, protozoa and nematodes to earthworms and arthropods. It even includes some snakes and burrowing mammals such as gophers, moles and prairie dogs. These organisms break down {{ref:soil-found-045}}, releasing nutrients for plants. In doing so they strongly shape the soil's fertility, plant growth, soil structure and carbon storage. Soil life powers the nutrient cycles. Without it, organic material would pile up as undecayed litter, with no dark, stable residue formed and no nutrients available to plants. Soil life also guards what it gathers: nitrogen and phosphorus held in its bodies are kept from leaching away. Microbial exudates help hold soil structure together, and earthworms mix the soil as they burrow. For all that, soil biology is a relatively new science with much still unknown. The discovery of {{ref:soil-bio-121}} in 1996 showed that basic questions about soil biogeochemical cycles remained open.

soil-bio-011.title: Soil microbiology and the 33,000 species on a beet root
soil-bio-011.text: In 2011, researchers detected more than 33,000 bacterial and archaeal species on the roots of sugar beet. Soil microbiology studies such microorganisms: what they do and how they affect soil properties. Its subjects are grouped as bacteria, including cyanobacteria and actinomycetes, archaea, fungi, algae, slime molds and protozoa. Their history is long. The first cyanobacteria arose two to four billion years ago. They fixed carbon and nitrogen, releasing oxygen into the air and nitrogen into the soil. How diverse a soil's microbes are depends on its pH, texture, soil organic matter content, plant community and contaminants such as heavy metals. That diversity pays off. Microbes make soil nutrients more available to plants, produce growth hormones, stimulate plant immunity and trigger or dampen plant stress responses. A more diverse soil microbiome, the whole community of soil microbes, generally brings fewer plant diseases and higher crop yields. The microbes also signal to one another through soluble metabolites, volatile organic compounds and extracellular polysaccharides. They trade metabolites that support each other's growth. Farmers can encourage them: sowing {{ref:soil-agri-066}} raises microbial activity, improving nitrogen availability, crop nitrogen uptake and yields.

soil-bio-063.title: Biomineralization: life that builds with stone
soil-bio-063.text: Every major lineage of living things has members that make minerals. Biomineralization is the process by which organisms produce or retain inorganic minerals, often to harden or stiffen their tissues. Over 60 different minerals have been identified in organisms. Most are silicates, carbonates or phosphates. Algae, diatoms and sponges build with silica, invertebrates with carbonates, and vertebrates with calcium phosphates and carbonates. Calcium phosphate and carbonate salts are the most common. Paired with organic polymers such as collagen and chitin, they give bones and shells their structural support. Microbes work on a geological scale. Bacteria take part in forming copper, iron and gold deposits, and microorganisms can both precipitate metals from solution and catalyze the dissolution of minerals. Soil sits inside a planetary loop. Bicarbonate released by weathering travels through soil to the sea, where it is turned into carbonate minerals for shells and skeletons. That makes biomineralization a store that locks carbon away, and a force in biogeochemical cycles. It can even clean up pollution. Microbes that release phosphate precipitate uranium phosphate minerals in contaminated groundwater, so the uranium moves less. The first evidence of biomineralization dates to some 750 million years ago, and organisms have made mineralized skeletons for the past 550 million years.

soil-bio-008.title: Five hundred sheep beneath a football pitch
soil-bio-008.text: The organisms living beneath a football pitch are estimated to equal the size of 500 sheep. Soil biodiversity is the relationship between soil and that variety of life, including the aspects of soil that can be managed with it in mind. Soil is chiefly a habitat for microbes such as bacteria and fungi. It also houses tiny animals such as protozoa and nematodes, small ones such as microarthropods and potworms, and larger ones such as earthworms, termites and millipedes. Their primary role is to recycle dead organic material from the plant-based food web above ground. In turn, their activity is a primary factor in how soil forms, physically and chemically. The link shows on maps: natural and farm vegetation boundaries closely follow soil boundaries, even at continental and global scales. Microbial exudates are now accepted as the main force that binds soil particles into clumps and shields carbon from further breakdown. Soil health depends on this diversity. Living covers on the soil and carbon-containing amendments improve it. {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, crop diversification, legume intercrops and organic inputs all correlate with more diverse soil life.

soil-bio-078.title: Burning a sample to measure its organic carbon
soil-bio-078.text: To count the organic carbon in a sample, a lab burns it. Total organic carbon is that analytical measure: the concentration of organic carbon present. The carbon is oxidized to carbon dioxide, for example by combustion at 1000 to 1200 °C or on a catalyst at 680 to 950 °C. Most modern analyzers read the gas by non-dispersive infrared. They measure only total carbon, which adds inorganic carbon, such as that in carbonate minerals, to the organic part. So the inorganic share is subtracted, or driven off first with acid. Soil organic matter content can be calculated from the result, and in the UK, guideline values for pollutants such as phenol and toluene depend on it. The measure also serves as a general indicator of water quality and as the first chemical test on potential petroleum source rock.

soil-bio-005.title: Why ecologists treat soil as an ecosystem
soil-bio-005.text: Soil organisms live under constant threat of drying out. Soil ecology studies how they interact with one another and with their environment. It is especially concerned with nutrient cycling, the formation of soil aggregates and soil biodiversity. Because soil is so complex and internally connected, soil ecologists regard it as an ecosystem in its own right. It is an uneven mix of minerals and soil organic matter, and its variations in structure, nutrients, moisture, temperature and pH support different organisms. Moisture is a major limit, and microbial communities shift through cycles of drying and rewetting. Temperature swings less with depth and governs microbial and enzyme activity, the release of nutrients and the pace of decay. Most soil organisms need oxygen. Microbes grow in air-filled micropores, while larger animals need macropores or water films to move. Patchy soils across a landscape, and changes between horizons, make communities patchy and layered with depth. Yet soil organisms remain underrepresented in studies and models, partly from an assumption that much below-ground diversity is ecologically redundant.

soil-bio-060.title: Oligotrophs, the slow specialists of scarcity
soil-bio-060.text: Some life thrives on almost nothing. An oligotroph is an organism able to live where nutrients are available only at very low levels. The word joins the Greek oligos, 'few', and trophikos, 'feeding'. Oligotrophs are contrasted with {{ref:soil-bio-088}}, organisms that prefer nutrient-rich settings. They grow slowly, run low metabolic rates and generally live at low population densities. Their homes have very low concentrations of nitrates, iron, phosphates and carbon sources: deep ocean sediments, caves, polar ice, aquifers, deep subsurface soil and leached soils. They cope with scarcity by switching on genes during lean periods. A feast is a problem: excess nutrients overwhelm their metabolism, and their enzymes struggle in rich conditions. Lichens, with their extremely low metabolic rate, and the cave-dwelling olm are examples. Rising carbon dioxide could favor them. It would speed plant and microbial growth but slow the cycling of carbon in soil, rewarding slower, more resource-efficient oligotrophs.

soil-bio-020.title: Why so many animals choose life underground
soil-bio-020.text: About 30% of all arthropods live in soil. Soil animals are those that spend their whole life there, or at least their larval stage. The soil shelters them from swings in temperature and moisture and from predators. It supplies food all year and a safe place to lay eggs. By body size they fall into four classes: 20 μm to 200 μm, 200 μm to 2 mm, 2 mm to 2 cm, and more than 2 cm. Size sets an animal's place in the {{ref:soil-bio-025}}, since bigger species eat smaller ones or reshape their surroundings. Many bear the marks of underground life. They tend to be smaller, blind, unpigmented, legless or short-legged, and often reproduce asexually. They are tightly bound to microbes, which feed them and help digest tough compounds. In return, the animals' guts, feces and cavities house microbes, spread them and regulate their numbers. Soil may even have been a crucible for the evolution of land invertebrates, a step between life in water and life in air. Studying them is slow. Each animal must be extracted, expelled, trapped or hand-sorted, then named by a specialist. DNA barcoding now yields full species lists, cryptic species included. One question stays open: researchers still debate whether and how fertilizers affect soil animals. In the sources, {{ref:soil-fert-010}} raised soil animal numbers while mineral fertilizers did not.

soil-bio-040.title: The earthworm, which Darwin ranked among history's great movers
soil-bio-040.text: In 1881 Charles Darwin wrote that few other animals had played so important a part in the history of the world. He meant the earthworm, a soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida. The name covers the largest members of the Oligochaeta. Earthworms live mostly in moist, compost-rich soil. They eat the remains of dead plants and animals, along with protozoa, nematodes, bacteria, fungi and algae, and rank among nature's most important eaters of dead matter. Adults range from 10 mm to 3 m long, though the typical common earthworm grows to about 360 mm. A worm moves by waves of muscle contraction, anchored by bristles called setae. It has no special respiratory organs and breathes through its moist skin. Populations depend on soil temperature, moisture, pH, salts, aeration and texture. Most favor neutral to slightly acidic soils, and their activity can shift pH to suit them. As they feed and burrow they aerate and mix the soil, help release nutrients for plants to take up, and bind soil organic matter to soil minerals. That makes them indicators of soil health. Healthy soil holds more of them, and their gut microbes reveal its condition. They are also vulnerable. {{ref:soil-fert-007}} create acidity fatal to worms, and pesticides kill them. At least three species are listed as extinct and many more as endangered.

soil-bio-052.title: Detritivores, the shredders that keep litter from piling up
soil-bio-052.text: Dead leaves and stems do not pile up in nature, and detritivores are the reason. A detritivore is a heterotroph, an organism that must eat to get its carbon, that feeds on {{ref:soil-bio-112}}: decomposing plant and animal parts and feces. It swallows discrete lumps of matter. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi instead absorb their food at a molecular scale, and the two terms are often confused. Typical soil detritivores include millipedes, {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, woodlice, slugs and many worms. They do the first stage of returning dead matter to mineral form, fragmenting plant remains so decomposers can complete the second. Together the two groups return carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium and potassium to the soil for plants. They keep litter moving even though cellulose, xylan and other woody compounds decay much more slowly than other organic molecules. Oddly, these feeders mainly digest the protein-rich microbes growing on dead matter and excrete the dead matter itself little changed. Moist soil increases their feeding. In deserts they shelter in burrows and are the main clearers of fallen plant matter. The past shows a world without full decay. In the Carboniferous, fungi and bacteria could not yet digest {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, so dead plant tissue piled up and later became fossil fuels.

soil-bio-025.title: The soil food web, a digestive system for the land
soil-bio-025.text: All soil organic matter passes through a living gut of sorts. The soil food web is the community of organisms living all or part of their lives in soil. It is seen as a network of feeding links that passes energy among them. A food chain follows one linear energy pathway; a food web shows all the potential pathways. Plants are the producers. Using sunlight, they make plant material from carbon dioxide and minerals, and their roots exude acids, sugars and enzymes that feed the web underground. Its members range from bacteria, algae, fungi and protozoa to nematodes and microarthropods, and on to earthworms, insects and small vertebrates. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break dead plant and animal material into simple nutrients. In this way the web processes dead material much as a digestive system processes food. The work reaches beyond the soil. The web keeps manure, plant residues and pesticides out of water, holds nitrogen back from groundwater, fixes nitrogen and helps water soak in. Its members prey on crop pests and feed animals above ground. Once thought simple, soil food webs turned out to have common omnivory and long, complex chains. Those chains still resist drying, freezing and fumigation. Some influence escapes the diagram, though. Litter transformers, mutualists and {{ref:soil-bio-004}} strongly affect their communities in ways food webs do not capture.

soil-bio-033.title: Soil respiration: the ground breathes out carbon
soil-bio-033.text: Each year the world's soils release an estimated 77 Pg of carbon, more than human sources such as fossil fuel burning. That flow is soil respiration: the carbon dioxide produced by respiring roots, the microbes around them and soil animals below ground. It is a key ecosystem process. Carbon fixed by photosynthesis returns to the air as CO2, respired either by roots or by the heterotrophs that consume plant material. Rates vary enormously with temperature, moisture, nutrient content and oxygen. Inside soil aggregates, oxygen gradients create anoxic microsites, tiny oxygen-free pockets where anaerobic metabolism dominates. Decaying litter is a major part of the total. It releases CO2 while locking up or freeing nutrients, so respiration rates track microbial turnover and the release of mineral nitrogen. Turning the soil with {{ref:soil-agri-095}} usually increases soil respiration, depleting soil organic matter. The stakes are global. Soils hold up to 3150 Pg of carbon, more than four times the atmosphere, so a small change in soil respiration can upset the balance of atmospheric CO2. Between 1989 and 2008 soil respiration rose by about 0.1% per year. Respiration also forms a positive feedback with climate: warming raises it, and so raises CO2. A 2 °C rise is estimated to add 10 Pg of carbon a year from soils.

soil-bio-041.title: Litter dwellers, soil eaters and deep diggers
soil-bio-041.text: Not all earthworms live the same life. Ecologists group them by where they live and feed into three categories: epigeic, endogeic and anecic. Epigeic worms live in leaf litter or compost where litter meets soil. They do not burrow, and they eat decaying plant and animal matter; Eisenia fetida is one. Because they eat fresh waste without burrowing and tolerate the heat of compost heaps, epigeic Eisenia species suit {{ref:soil-bio-044}}. Endogeic worms live in topsoil or subsoil. They eat soil itself and dig horizontal burrows in the upper 10–30 cm. Anecic worms, whose name means 'reaching up', include the common earthworm. They build permanent, deep vertical burrows and come up to gather leaves. In doing so they mix surface plant matter into the mineral soil below. The categories help in judging land. Healthy soil holds a larger number and biomass of earthworms, especially endogeic and anecic species.

soil-bio-042.title: How earthworms turn leaf fall into fertile soil
soil-bio-042.text: Darwin estimated up to 53,000 worms per acre of cropland. Newer figures run from 250,000 per acre on poor soil to 1,750,000 per acre on rich farmland. Richly organic topsoil averages 500 earthworms per square meter, weighing up to 400 g/m2. All those worms improve soil for plants by fragmenting, mixing, grinding and digesting plant debris. Anecic worms pull leaf fall and manure into their burrows, shred it and mix it with soil, turning it into {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. Their casts can hold 40 percent more of it than the top 230 mm of soil. Grit in the gizzard grinds swallowed particles, sand grains up to 1.3 mm included, into a paste whose large surface favors microbes and enzymes. Casts are richer in carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus than the surrounding soil, with nutrients in forms plants can use. On rich ground, one worm may produce over 4.5 kilograms of casts a year. Burrows keep soil structured, aerated and drained, and worms speed the formation of water-stable macroaggregates, large crumbs that hold together when wet. Their effect on carbon was long debated: do worms hasten its loss as CO2, or preserve it? A consensus now credits them with storing carbon, since most is stabilized deep in the soil with clay. Their greenhouse gas emissions, direct or through soil microbes, are not yet fully quantified but likely add to global warming.

soil-bio-074.title: Petrichor, the smell of rain on dry ground
soil-bio-074.text: Pliny the Elder noticed the pleasant smell of earth when rain follows drought, and took it as a sign of fertile soil. That earthy scent now has a name: petrichor. Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Grenfell Thomas introduced the term in a 1964 Nature paper, replacing the older 'argillaceous odour'. They built it from the Greek petra, rock, and ichor, the fluid in the veins of the gods. The smell is a mixture of volatiles. In dry spells, oils from plant matter build up on mineral surfaces. Moisture pushes them out of rock and soil pores, joined by the microbial compounds {{ref:soil-bio-075}} and 2-methylisoborneol. The scent offers a glimpse of the soil atmosphere, because infiltrating rain flushes out the soil air after a drought. Pinning it down took time. In 1891 Marcellin Berthelot and G. André steam-distilled an odorous substance from soil but could not identify it. In 1965 Bear and Thomas reported that small amounts of the oily extracts delay seed germination and early plant growth. High-speed filming at MIT in 2015 showed raindrops on porous surfaces trapping air bubbles that burst as aerosols. Light or moderate rain made more aerosols than heavy rain. A 2026 study in dryland soils reaching into the Negev Desert found 58 volatile organic compounds released on rewetting, which may feed atmospheric ozone and secondary aerosol formation.

soil-bio-039.title: Soil enzymes, the chemical tools of decay
soil-bio-039.text: Microbes face a problem of scale: much of their food comes as large molecules left by dead plants and animals. Soil enzymes solve it. Released mainly by microbes, they break down soil organic matter and free nutrients for plants. Fungi, bacteria and archaea excrete them, and plant roots produce some. They speed the breakdown of compounds such as cellulose, starch and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, which makes them prominent agents of the carbon and nitrogen cycles. Some work inside cells, some stay attached to cells, and some float free. Enzymes bound to clay and humic particles are protected from rapid breakdown but are less active, a trade-off between protection and activity. Their spread is highly patchy, varying at the millimeter scale with nutrients, microbes and roots, and from single trees to whole catchments. Farming steers them. Some fertilizers include {{ref:soil-fert-085}}, which hold back the enzyme that breaks down that compound so nutrients are released over a longer period. Enzyme activity was higher with manure than with inorganic fertilizer, though other studies found a mix of mineral and organic inputs better still. Enzymes both stabilize and degrade soil structure, and they play a decisive role in keeping soil healthy.

soil-bio-002.title: Billions in a teaspoon: the bacteria of the soil
soil-bio-002.text: A teaspoon of productive soil holds 100 million to 3 billion bacteria. In and around plant roots, up to 10 billion culturable cells live in each gram. Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes, cells without a nucleus, and they are the soil's most numerous inhabitants. They live in soil water, including the moisture film around particles, where some swim with whip-like flagella. When conditions suit, they multiply fast by splitting in two. Most beneficial soil bacteria need oxygen and are most active in moist but unsaturated soil of neutral pH with plenty of food. Those that live without oxygen tend to putrefy dead plant and animal matter. Away from roots, most rest as drought-resistant colonies in a polysaccharide matrix coated with clay platelets. They wait until {{ref:soil-bio-142}} or earthworm mucus reach them. Hostile conditions send them dormant: Gram-positive Bacillus and Clostridium form spores, and Gram-negative bacteria enter a resting stage in which they cannot be cultured. Bacteria run key steps of the {{ref:soil-fert-099}}. Some capture nitrogen from the air, some turn ammonia toward nitrate, and others return nitrate to gas where oxygen is absent. Pseudomonas can metabolize a wide range of chemicals, while {{ref:soil-fert-147}} gets its energy only by oxidizing nitrite to nitrate. Soil archaea, also prokaryotes, are still poorly known but may matter in that ammonia-to-nitrate step and in methanogenesis. Some bacteria colonize minerals and speed their weathering.

soil-bio-075.title: Geosmin, the earthy molecule noses catch in traces
soil-bio-075.text: People can smell geosmin at just 0.006 to 0.01 micrograms per liter of water. Geosmin is a chemical with a distinct earthy or musty smell, made by bacteria common in soil and water. Its name joins the Greek geō-, 'earth', and osmē, 'smell'. Nancy N. Gerber and Hubert A. Lechevalier coined it in 1965 after isolating it from actinomycete cultures, and Gerber worked out its structure in 1968. It is a secondary metabolite, a by-product rather than a necessity of life, of cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Phormidium and Planktothrix and of actinomycetes, mainly Streptomyces. It gives beetroot its earthy taste and contributes to petrichor. The natural (−) form is about eight times more potent than the other, with a mean threshold of 9.5 ng/L against 78 ng/L. With 2-methylisoborneol it is the main biological cause of muddy tastes in drinking water and farmed fish worldwide. It is nontoxic to humans and breaks down in acid, yet standard water treatment cannot remove it, so suppliers need combined methods such as advanced oxidation. In the soil it carries signals. It attracts {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, which feed on Streptomyces and spread its spores, and it repels the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.

soil-bio-003.title: Seven hundred kilometers of fungal thread in a gram of soil
soil-bio-003.text: A gram of garden soil can hold around one million fungi and around 700 km of fungal threads, called hyphae. Soil fungi are the yeasts, molds and other fungi of the soil. They lack chlorophyll, spread through the soil as a web of threads called mycelium, and feed on dead plant and animal matter. Bacteria may outnumber them in cell counts, but fungi can contribute more biomass and respiration in some soils. As chemo-heterotrophs, they need organic substrates for their carbon. Their mycelium breaks fresh remains down into {{ref:soil-bio-089}} and carbon dioxide. In that work the key fungi are saprotrophs, which turn dead matter into mineral forms such as nitrate, ammonium and phosphate that plants can use. Dead matter is colonized by a succession of species: sugar and starch users first, then those able to break down cellulose and tougher woody compounds. Many fungi are parasites that cause plant disease. Others are beneficial partners, such as {{ref:soil-bio-157}}, and fungi also help bind soil into crumbs and feed larger soil organisms. Compared with bacteria, fungi fare relatively well in acidic soils and in dry soils, which hold more of the oxygen they need. Fruiting bodies such as mushrooms release spores that spread by wind, water and fungus-eating animals and can lie dormant for years.

openers.bio: Beneath every field and forest lives a crowd of microbes and animals, and this part of the course is about them. Soil biology studies their activity and ecology, while soil microbiology narrows the lens to the microorganisms and how they change soil properties. About 30% of arthropods live in soil, alongside earthworms and the detritivores that eat decomposing plant and animal parts and feces. Soil ecology traces how these organisms interact, and the soil food web maps the feeding links that pass energy among them. All that life breathes, too: soil respiration is the carbon dioxide given off by roots, microbes and soil animals below ground.
openers.life-in-the-soil: Some organisms scrape by where nutrients are barely present; others harden their own tissues with minerals. This chapter meets them both, starting with the sciences that study soil life and the variety of that life. Its cast runs from microbes to earthworms, the largest members of the Oligochaeta, and to the detritivores that eat decaying plant and animal parts. A simple lab measure, total organic carbon, shows how much organic carbon a sample holds. Feeding links, mineral-making and the carbon dioxide that soil life breathes out show what all these organisms do together.
